articles.title: A safer hydrogenation strategy using poly( p -phenylene sulfide)-supported Pd catalysts for the chemoselective reduction of α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compounds
articles.abstract: A palladium catalyst supported on porous poly( p -phenylene sulfide) (Pd(0)/PPS) was developed for the chemoselective hydrogenation of α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compounds.

articles.title: Long-range actin-driven endosymbiont mobility in an animal-algal symbiosis
articles.abstract: Hundreds to thousands of dinoflagellate symbionts (Amphidinium sp., 10–20 μm in size) move up to hundreds of micrometers inside the tissue of their acoel worm hosts (Waminoa sp., millimeters in size). Host actin machinery is primarily responsible for driving symbiont mobility at speeds around 1 μm/s, and symbionts move inside ribbon-like host cells (∼200 nm thin), which stretch to accommodate symbionts moving through them.

articles.title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington’s disease
articles.abstract: By using multimodal spatial transcriptomics to measure somatic repeat expansion, huntingtin pathology, and transcriptional profile in every cell of intact tissue sections, we identify in the Huntington’s disease cortex that large somatic CAG repeat expansions are linked to the selective loss of L5–6 NP and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons. Intranuclear inclusions of huntingtin were most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansions and were associated with broader transcriptional changes than somatic repeat expansion alone.

articles.title: Somatic DNA-repeat expansions initiate distinct yet analogous changes in Huntington’s disease cortical and striatal neurons
articles.abstract: Single-cell-resolution analysis of brain tissue in Huntington's disease (HD) reveals that cortical and striatal neurons pass through analogous biological changes, each initiated by a neuron's own expanding DNA repeat. In cortical neurons, as in striatal neurons, the DNA repeat expands somatically over decades (phases A and B) and becomes toxic at about 150 CAGs, initiating cell-identity erosion (phase C), the formation of nuclear inclusions of aggregated HTT protein, a derepression crisis (phase D), and then death of the neuron.

articles.title: Sleep-dependent DNA methylation remodeling in basolateral amygdala fear engrams
articles.abstract: How sleep consolidates fear memories at the molecular level within individual engram neurons is unknown. Using activity-dependent tagging and sequencing, we profiled the DNA methylome and transcriptome of engram and non-engram nuclei from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) after contextual fear conditioning with and without post-learning sleep deprivation. Fear learning induces coordinated CpG and CpH DNA methylation remodeling specifically in engram neurons, with each showing unique temporal dynamics, revealing CpH methylation as a separate component of the engram's epigenetic signature. Interestingly, sleep deprivation partially reverses learning-induced methylation changes and impairs memory recall, indicating that sleep supports engram-specific epigenetic consolidation. Integrating the engram methylome with single-cell transcriptome profiling, we construct a multi-omic molecular atlas of the BLA fear engram and identify Mid1 as a learning- and sleep-regulated methylation target. BLA-wide and engram-specific Mid1 knockdown establishes its functional requirement for fear memory consolidation, providing an approach to identify behaviorally relevant epigenetic targets.

articles.title: Stress hyperglycemia impairs FOXK2-dependent macrophage cardiac repair after myocardial infarction
articles.abstract: Stress hyperglycemia (SHG) predicts poor outcomes after myocardial infarction (MI), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify FOXK2 as a key regulator of macrophage-mediated cardiac repair. FOXK2 expression was reduced in cardiac macrophages from hyperglycemic mice after MI and in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with MI with SHG, whereas macrophage-specific FOXK2 deficiency aggravated cardiac injury. Under high-glucose conditions, FOXK2 was glycosylated at T552 by O-GlcNAc transferase, promoting its ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent degradation. Mass spectrometry and functional assays showed that the FOXK2T552A variant resisted hyperglycemia-induced degradation. Integrated CUT&Tag and RNA-seq analyses revealed that FOXK2 restrained pro-inflammatory cytokine expression by suppressing H3K27 acetylation. Thus, our findings identify FOXK2 as a critical regulator that supports cardiac repair during hyperglycemia, and targeting excessive FOXK2 O-GlcNAcylation may offer a therapeutic strategy for patients with MI and SHG.

articles.title: Moving beyond overconfidence: A clinical roadmap for integrating uncertainty-aware AI models into medical workflows
articles.abstract: Luo et al. review uncertainty quantification in medical AI from a clinical perspective and propose a practical roadmap for translating uncertainty estimates into meaningful action. They highlight the need to validate uncertainty against clinically relevant errors and embed its use within real-world workflows and governance.

articles.title: Tailoring bandgap and electron affinity of spacecraft dielectrics for synergistic solar array charging and discharge suppression
EPCR expression marks CD150neg deeply dormant long-term hematopoietic stem cells
articles.abstract: Lin et al. identified a distinct EPCR+CD150− hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) subset termed LT-HSC2. It is characterized by a prominent dormancy status during homeostasis that surpasses EPCR+CD150+ LT-HSC1. LT-HSC2s exhibit all LT-HSC hallmarks including extensive capacity to self-renew and serial multi-lineage reconstitution capacity at bulk and single-cell level.

articles.title: Electroconductive patch promotes heart repair by directing epicardial cells toward endothelial fate
articles.abstract: Qiu and colleagues revealed that the endothelial potential of adult EPDCs is unlocked by an improved electroconductive microenvironment rebuilt through cardiac electroconductive-matched patches. Using lineage tracing and scRNA-seq, they explored how electroconductive microenvironment guides EPDCs into functional vessels, promoting cardiac repair post-MI.

articles.title: Organoids and organs-on-a-chip as new approach methodologies at the convergence of cell biology and bioengineering
articles.abstract: Human tissue models are rewriting preclinical science. Tavakol et al. examine how converging cell biology and bioengineering can close translational gaps, overcome reproducibility and regulatory hurdles, and, with synthetic biology, multi-omics, and AI, turn organoids and organs-on-a-chip into foundational platforms for personalized medicine, drug discovery, and regenerative therapies.

articles.title: In situ/operando Mössbauer spectroscopy in single-atom catalysis: From structure-activity relationships to dynamic mechanisms
articles.abstract: In situ/operando and rapid freeze-quench Mössbauer approaches enable quantitative tracking of the oxidation state, spin state, and local coordination environment of Mössbauer-active metal sites in single-atom catalysts during catalytic processes, thus providing a deeper understanding of dynamic reaction mechanisms and contributing to the rational design of novel, efficient catalysts at the atomic scale.

articles.title: Engineering Reversible Wet Adhesion: Physicochemical Principles from Molecular Interactions to Functional Biointerfaces
articles.abstract: Interfacial hydration fundamentally constrains adhesion in aqueous and physiological environments by preventing intimate contact, competing for binding sites, and weakening the load-bearing interfaces. Although wet adhesives have been extensively designed for durable fixation, emerging technologies in soft robotics, wearable bioelectronics, and minimally invasive medicine require interfaces that can form adhesion, recover after reuse, or detach on-demand under hydrated conditions. This Review discusses reversible wet adhesion through two operational modes: Mode I, cyclic reusability through repeated restoration of adhesion over attachment-detachment cycles, and Mode II, on-demand detachability through trigger-induced conversion of a stable adhesive state into a weakly adherent state through a controlled, low-damage release pathway. We examine supramolecular interactions, dynamic covalent chemistry, mesoscale architectures, biomimetic designs, and hybrid strategies as complementary routes for regulating hydration, interfacial binding, mechanical dissipation, and adhesive state transitions at wet interfaces. We analyze how contact formation, hydration history, fracture pathways, loading history, test geometry, and biofluid exposure shape the measured performance. We further assess current methods for quantifying reusability, switching, durability, and biofluid tolerance, emphasizing failure mode-informed evaluation and standardized reporting criteria. Integrating hydration thermodynamics, binding kinetics, mechanical dissipation, and stimulus-gated interfacial transitions, this Review develops design and evaluation principles for reversible wet adhesive systems in complex aqueous and biointerfacial environments.

articles.title: High-Entropy Materials for Electrochemical Gas Conversion
articles.abstract: High-entropy materials (HEMs) are composed of multiple principal elements stabilized by the configurational entropy. They establish a new design paradigm in electrocatalysis by leveraging local disorder and multielement synergy to create diverse and tunable active site environments. While HEMs have been broadly reviewed, a focused and reaction-specific assessment of their role in gas-involved electrocatalysis is absent. This review fills that gap by examining entropy-driven design principles, entropy-guided synthesis, nanoscale structural control, and advanced characterization of HEMs and by linking these aspects to their reaction-specific catalytic behavior in gas-involved electrocatalysis. We build a unified framework linking high-entropy chemistry to catalytic function across five key reactions: the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR), oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR), and nitrogen oxidation reaction (NOR). We provide comprehensive coverage across all major HEM families, including high-entropy alloys, oxides, chalcogenides, hydroxides, fluorides, MXenes, and single-atom configurations, highlighting features unique to each system. Key challenges and future directions are outlined, including scalable synthesis, active-site identification, machine-learning-guided discovery, and interfacial engineering. This review provides a reaction-focused framework for advancing HEM-based electrocatalysis and offers guidance for designing next-generation materials for clean energy technologies.

articles.title: Introduction: Fabrication at All Scales
Design guidelines for body-conformable aqueous zinc-based batteries
articles.abstract: This review outlines design principles, printing methods, stretchable electrodes, structural strategies, and cathode chemistries for body-conformable aqueous zinc-based batteries in medical devices.

articles.title: Label-free Raman spectroscopy for cancer therapy response: from methodological framework to clinical translation
articles.abstract: This review critically connects Raman modalities, molecular readouts, data analysis and clinical translation for cancer therapy-response studies.

articles.title: Atomate2-ARTATOP: High-Throughput Screening and the Atomic-Level Origin of Second Harmonic Generation in Phosphorus Chalcogenides
articles.abstract: While phosphorus chalcogenides are promising candidates for infrared nonlinear optical (IR-NLO) applications, a fundamental understanding of the microscopic mechanisms driving their second harmonic generation (SHG) response is still lacking. In this work, we address this gap by developing atomate2-ARTATOP, an open-source high-throughput computational framework that integrates atomic response theory (ART) into atomate2 to enable systematic NLO property screening and analysis. Our large-scale screening of 231 non-centrosymmetric compounds spanning thiophosphates (PS), selenophosphates (PSe), and oxygen-containing phosphorus chalcogenides (PSO) reveals a clear SHG performance trend (PSe > PS > PSO), mapping specific chemical families to targeted infrared and ultraviolet spectral windows. Notably, Hg2P2S7 and InPSe4 exhibit exceptional powder-averaged SHG coefficients of 29.15 (∼2.8 × AGS) and 34.28 pm/V (∼3.2 × AGS), respectively, outperforming the industry standard AgGaS2. Interestingly, unlike conventional thiophosphates, ZnGaPS, a mixed phosphide-sulfide, also exhibits a strong SHG response (21.4 pm/V, ∼2.0 × AGS). Additionally, we identify P2S2O3 as a superior ultraviolet candidate, combining a wide band gap (5.35 eV) with an SHG response ∼7.8 times that of KH2PO4. Through partial response function analysis, we demonstrate that the SHG response is fundamentally governed by nonbonding chalcogen p states, with other elements playing a secondary role on average but contributing considerably in individual compounds. Moreover, the net response in many compounds reflects a competition between positive and negative contributions from different structural units. Finally, by identifying compositional features that induce negative SHG contributions, we offer design insights for enhancing constructive SHG contributions. This work provides a quantitative, orbital-level blueprint for the discovery of next-generation NLO materials.

articles.title: Discovery of Structurally Diverse Zintl Polyphosphides (Eu,Sr)P x by Computationally Assisted High-Pressure Synthesis
articles.abstract: Phosphorus exhibits rich allotropy that gives rise to diverse polyanionic clusters and networks. The unusual transport phenomena observed in black phosphorus and its magnetic analogue α-EuP3 highlight the potential of extended phosphorus networks to generate emergent electronic properties. At the same time, high pressure has a natural affinity with P-rich polyphosphides, as it offers access to structurally diverse phosphorus networks, presenting them as a promising platform for materials discovery. In this work, P-rich compounds in the Sr−P and Eu−P systems were explored by combining high-pressure synthesis with first-principles calculations. Five previously unknown polyphosphides were synthesized across the P-rich composition range AP8−AP10 (A = Eu, Sr): EuP8, EuP9, EuP10, SrP8, and SrP10. These compounds contain chain-like and cage-like phosphorus frameworks, with varying lone-pair-bearing P concentrations across compositions. Pressure-dependent convex-hull calculations incorporating the experimentally determined structures identify a narrow moderate pressure window of 2−4 GPa in which the discovered P-rich phases become synthetically accessible, thereby providing a practical guide to their high-pressure synthesis conditions. These results demonstrate that computationally assisted high-pressure synthesis provides a powerful approach to discovering unexplored metastable phases and developing magnetic and topological functionalities in anion-rich binary Zintl compounds.

articles.title: Effects of Oxygen Adsorption and Temperature on Lead Telluride Surfaces
articles.abstract: As a traditional thermoelectric material, PbTe exhibits a high peak zT value. However, it is highly susceptible to oxidation during either synthesis or device operation. Thus, it is essential to understand the oxidation behavior at finite temperatures and its effects on the geometries of PbTe surfaces. Focusing on oxygen adsorption at two stable PbTe(100) and PbTe(111) surfaces, using cluster expansion, we identify the most stable adsorption configurations of 0.5O−PbTe(100) and 0.33O−PbTe(111) with oxygen coverages of 0.5 and 0.33, respectively. Electronic structure calculations reveal that oxygen atoms form covalent bonds with surface Te atoms. Ab initio molecular dynamics investigations demonstrate temperature is a critical factor that damages PbTe surfaces and drives oxygen atoms into sublayers, forming surface oxides. Oxygen atoms migrate into a deeper sublayer on PbTe(111) than on PbTe(100). Increasing temperature and oxygen coverage aggravate these effects. Surface oxidation fundamentally deteriorates electrical transport characteristics by changing carrier concentration, inducing transitions between n- and p-type conduction, and decreasing carrier mobility. This ultimately leads to significant degradation in its thermoelectric performance. Possible approaches include depositing dense passivation layers to block oxygen adsorption and diffusion.

articles.title: Hierarchically Porous Polyaniline Film via Interfacial Self-Assembly for Ultrafast Dual-Band Electrochromic Smart Window
articles.abstract: Dual-band electrochromic smart windows, capable of independently regulating visible and near-infrared solar radiation, offer an effective route toward reducing building/vehicle energy consumption. However, their practical implementation is often limited by slow switching kinetics, insufficient bistability, as well as challenges in fabricating polychromatic, uniform, and scalable electrochromic films with efficient ion and charge transport. Here, we report an interfacial self-assembly strategy to fabricate large-area polyaniline (PANI) thin films featuring a hierarchically porous architecture and thickness-dependent porosity gradient. The self-assembly process, driven by solvent exchange at the air–water interface and modulated by surfactant confinement, produces interconnected PANI nanoparticle networks with both in-plane hierarchical pores and out-of-plane structural gradation. This architecture facilitates electrolyte penetration and charge transport across the film thickness. As a result, the PANI films enable rapid and stable dual-band electrochromic modulation, exhibiting three distinct optical states (“bright”, “cool”, and “dark”) with independent control of visible and near-infrared transmittance. The assembled devices demonstrate fast response (coloration/bleaching times of 1.8/4 s at 633 nm and 1.2/3.6 s at 1200 nm), high coloration efficiency, and excellent optical bistability, together with effective indoor thermal regulation. These results establish interfacial self-assembly as a versatile approach for engineering functional polymer films for next-generation energy-efficient smart windows.

articles.title: High-Performance Ce-Doped HfO2 Ferroelectric Thin Films by Atomic Layer Deposition
articles.abstract: Ce-doped HfO2 (HCO) ferroelectric thin films have attracted considerable attention for next-generation integrated ferroelectric devices owing to their excellent compatibility with complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology and promising ferroelectric properties. However, previously reported HCO films generally require relatively large thicknesses and high processing temperatures, limiting their application in highly scaled devices. Here, we demonstrate HCO ferroelectric thin films grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) and systematically investigate the effects of Ce concentration and film thickness on their structural and ferroelectric properties. The HCO film with 5.0% Ce doping exhibits the highest ferroelectric orthorhombic phase fraction, which is attributed to the formation of coupled defects involving Ce-substitution on Hf sites and oxygen vacancies, as revealed by first-principles calculations. Moreover, the HCO films annealed at 700 °C exhibit excellent ferroelectric properties at the thickness ranging from 12 to 24 nm. In particular, the 18 nm-thick HCO film with 5.0% Ce achieves a remanent polarization of 19.4 μC/cm2 and an excellent switching endurance exceeding 1 × 109 cycles. These results demonstrate the potential of ALD-grown HCO as a scalable material platform for highly integrated and multifunctional ferroelectric devices.

articles.title: Ion Activity and Metal Ion Speciation Rationalize Outcomes in WO3 Nanoparticle Synthesis
articles.abstract: Acid-mediated precipitation of aqueous tungstate solutions is widely used to synthesize WO3 nanoparticles, yet the coupling of reagent identity, ionic strength, and speciation equilibria across different synthetic protocols cloud which variables govern resulting polymorph type and nanoparticle morphology, as well as whether polymorph and nanoparticle morphology can be tuned independently. Here, we systematically vary acid and alkali salt identity, alkali cation concentration, and acid addition rate to isolate their individual contributions. By accounting for differences in ion activities and speciation equilibria, we show that apparent structure-directing effects previously attributed to anion identity instead arise primarily from solution-level differences rather than direct anion−WO3 interactions. In contrast, alkali cation concentration exerts an independent influence on the favorability of the metastable hexagonal phase that persists even after accounting for differences in ionic strength and speciation. We further demonstrate that acid addition rate modulates nanoparticle morphology without affecting polymorph outcome, identifying acidification kinetics as a synthetic handle acting independently of the factors governing polymorph selection. Using these mechanistic insights, we then show the systematic tunability of polymorph-dependent photochromic behavior in the resulting particles. Together, these findings provide independent synthetic handles for controlling WO3 nanoparticle phase and morphology which directly impact their functional properties, and offer a quantitative approach for reconciling and comparing outcomes across diverse reagent combinations and protocols in WO3 NP synthesis.

articles.title: A Multi‐Tissue Transcriptomic Resource for the Brahminy Blindsnake Indotyphlops braminus (Squamata: Typhlopidae)
articles.abstract: The Brahminy blindsnake (Indotyphlops braminus), an all‐female, parthenogenetic, and triploid snake, is an informative species for studying polyploidy and asexual reproduction in vertebrates. In this study, we analyzed tissue expression patterns in I. braminus using a PacBio‐derived transcript reference and Illumina RNA‐seq. Differential expression and annotation over‐representation analyses were used to characterize tissue‐associated expression differences and over‐represented annotations across ovary, heart, liver, and skin from the same three individuals. The three overlapping eye‐spot pools were described at the library level. Weighted gene co‐expression network analysis (WGCNA) was used only as an exploratory analysis of the 12 four‐tissue libraries. A total of 835,353,682 clean read pairs were retained, and gene expression profiles showed broad differences among the four formally analyzed tissues. Of 30,224 tested genes, 13,849 showed a tissue effect, and 4228 candidate tissue‐enriched genes were identified by requiring higher expression in all three relevant pairwise comparisons. Six representative annotation terms remained significant in the sensitivity analysis, and 3 of 11 non‐gray co‐expression modules passed the prespecified stability rule across nine alternative networks. This study provides an additional multi‐tissue transcriptomic resource for I. braminus, with candidate sets that can guide future functional and comparative tests of hypotheses concerning parthenogenesis, triploidy, fossoriality, and visual reduction.

articles.title: Behavioral and Physiological Response of Eucosma giganteana to Semiochemicals From Conspecifics and Silphium integrifolium
articles.abstract: Eucosma giganteana is a specialist herbivore on Silphium spp. and a major limiting factor to the commercialization of Silphium integrifolium, a perennial oilseed crop. Although it is known that (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate works as an attractant to E. giganteana, it is unknown whether it responds in a concentration‐dependent manner, and whether this cue works throughout the season. Also unknown is whether these moths behaviorally or physiologically respond to other important semiochemicals, such as those emitted by conspecifics or its host. This information is important for developing volatiles for use in behaviorally‐based management of E. giganteana. To address our questions, we performed field trapping with traps baited with (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate, characterized headspace emissions from E. giganteana, and used EAG and flight mill analysis to assess response to (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate and volatiles derived from S. integrifolium and conspecifics. Higher loadings of (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate in the field trapping studies conducted in 2024 resulted in increased captures of E. giganteana moths on sticky traps, which successfully monitored E. giganteana through their full flight period. EAG showed antennal depolarizations, which confirmed E. giganteana perceive (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate. In addition, female E. giganteana perceive volatiles emitted by S. integrifolium whereas males did not. Despite eliciting clear antennal responses and showing success in field monitoring, (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate did not influence flight behavior during the flight mill experiments under the tested conditions. Altogether this study shows (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate successfully monitored E. giganteana through the field season; more work is required to deploy it in behaviorally‐based management IPM tactics.

articles.title: Cave‐Dwelling Planariidae in Dinaric Karst Exhibit Differing Levels of Cave Trait Evolution
articles.abstract: The Dinaric karst encompasses a network of over 10,000 caves and represents one of the world's most important subterranean biodiversity hotspots. It is inhabited by remarkably diverse and often endemic species, including planarian flatworms. Although cave planarians have long been known from the region, they have not yet been investigated using an integrative approach, and their evolutionary relationships with surface‐dwelling relatives remain unresolved. To address these gaps, we combined field sampling, phylogenetic analyses based on the COI and 18S genes, and phenotypic characterisation. Our results show that cave planariids in the Dinaric karst belong to at least three genera and are more widespread and diverse than previously assumed. We increased the number of cave records in the Dinaric karst from 26 to 37 and documented cf. Atrioplanaria and Phagocata in Croatian caves for the first time. Phylogenetic reconstructions are consistent with independent cave colonisation events, including multiple instances within the genera Crenobia and cf. Atrioplanaria. Variation in pigmentation and eye reduction, both within and between populations, further reveals heterogeneous evolutionary trajectories of cave‐associated phenotypes. Our molecular phylogeny and documentation of trait variability constitute a first step towards establishing Planariidae as a model for investigating the mechanisms underlying the convergent evolution of pigment loss and eye reduction in cave environments.

articles.title: Contrasting Associations of Urbanization and Lateral Hydrological Gradients With Functional Structure and Rarity of Spontaneous Plants in River Corridors: Evidence From Changde, China
articles.abstract: River corridors play an important role in maintaining the diversity and ecological functions of spontaneous plants. Within urban river corridors, spontaneous plant communities are exposed to both urbanization in the surrounding landscape and lateral hydrological variation between water and land. However, the relative contributions of the surrounding urban matrix and the lateral hydrological position to these community properties have rarely been examined within a common framework. Functional rarity was included because it complements conventional diversity metrics by identifying uncommon functional strategies. We surveyed spontaneous plants along six rivers and one lake in the central urban area of Changde, China, and combined analyses of plant functional traits with structural equation modeling to evaluate the associations of urbanization gradient and lateral hydrological gradient with species diversity, functional structure, and functional rarity. The results showed that species diversity (Shannon–Wiener) and functional diversity (FDis) showed unimodal patterns across urbanization levels, with the highest values at intermediate urbanization. Functional trait space was more clearly separated among lateral habitat types than among urbanization levels. Functional rarity increased with ISA but declined with WD. The structural equation models showed contrasting associations of the two gradients with community properties: higher ISA was associated with greater community‐weighted mean plant height and functional rarity but lower species diversity and FDis, whereas greater WD showed the opposite pattern. Functional rarity was positively associated with FDis in both models. This study provides a transferable framework for comparative research across urban river systems. The framework integrates urbanization at the landscape scale, lateral habitat variation within river corridors, and complementary species, functional, structural, and rarity metrics. The framework is helpful in identifying community patterns that assessments based on a single gradient or a single metric may overlook.

articles.title: Copy Number Variation‐Based Molecular Sexing of Ixodes scapularis and Rhipicephalus microplus Immature Stages Using qPCR and ddPCR Approaches
articles.abstract: Accurate sex identification of immature ticks is essential for understanding sex‐specific ecological dynamics, pathogen transmission, and reproductive biology. However, tick larvae and nymphs lack morphological sexual dimorphisms, limiting such studies. Here, we report the development and validation of a copy number variation (CNV)‐based molecular sexing approach for two important hard tick species: Ixodes scapularis, a major public health vector of human pathogens, and Rhipicephalus microplus, an ectoparasite responsible for significant economic losses in the cattle industry. Using newly published chromosomal‐level genome assemblies and whole‐genome resequencing data, we identified female‐enriched CNVs in two genes—calcium/calmodulin‐dependent 3′,5′‐cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase 1A‐like (NPD) and rap guanine nucleotide exchange factor 2‐like (RAPGEF2)—and developed SYBR‐Green and probe‐based qPCR and droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) assays using DNA extracted non‐destructively from a single leg, thus preserving ticks for continued feeding, molting, and behavioral analysis. In I. scapularis, we were able to assign the sex of 91.3% of nymphs based on results from at least two molecular tests, and these assignments were confirmed when the nymphs later molted into adults. Similarly, in R. microplus, the qPCR assay revealed clear, sex‐linked differences in gene copy number. Together, these findings indicate that CNV‐based markers are a reliable and widely applicable method for sex determination in immature ticks.

articles.title: Evaluating the Potential of Four Native Ziziphus Species for Restoring Savanna‐Like Habitats in Jinsha River Under Climate Change
articles.abstract: The Jinsha River, as the upper section of the Yangtze River, plays a key role as an ecological barrier, yet its dry‐hot valleys face severe degradation due to harsh climate and human activities. Four native Ziziphus species (Z. mauritiana, Z. montana, Z. mairei, and Z. xiangchengensis) were selected to assess their potential for restoring “valley‐type savanna” vegetation through field investigations, species distribution modeling, germination experiments, and interviews. Field investigations showed that Z. mairei and Z. xiangchengensis exhibit limited distributions and small populations, requiring artificial propagation and protection. MaxEnt models performed well (AUC > 0.9). Ziziphus montana occurs in northwestern Yunnan and is primarily limited by temperature seasonality (bio4), elevation, and coldest quarter temperature (bio11). Under future climate scenarios, its suitable habitat is projected to contract by 11.3%–20.4%, with the remaining highly suitable area retreating toward the Jinsha River basin. Bio11 is the primary factor influencing the distribution of Z. mauritiana, and its suitable range is projected to expand by 44.1%–119.1%. Seed heteromorphism was documented for the first time in Z. xiangchengensis, Z. montana, and Z. mairei, classified into Type A (2 carpels) and B (3 carpels) based on carpel number, with Type A seeds dominating (66.0%–94.8%). These two seed types showed significant differences in temperature response and dormancy characteristics. Four Ziziphus species displayed strong physical dormancy, removing the endocarp and cracking the seed coat results in a 100% germination rate, providing a practical solution for large‐scale seedling propagation. Based on assessment, Z. montana is more suitable for ecological restoration in the Jinsha River Basin. The population age structure is of the expanding type and serves medicinal, edible, agricultural, ecological restoration, and handicraft purposes. We advocate for community‐based “interactive” ecological restoration, using economic incentives to drive ecological recovery. This study contributes to ecological restoration, germplasm conservation, and local economic development.

articles.title: Genetic Analysis of Invasive Rats From the Hahajima Islands in the Ogasawara Islands
articles.abstract: Based on mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences, we concluded that the Hahajima Islands are largely inhabited by Rattus norvegicus (brown rat), except for Katsuodorijima. The previous study reported that the Chichijima Islands were occupied by Rattus rattus complex (RrC) (black rats). We considered that R. norvegicus inhabits the Hahajima Islands owing to a combination of factors, such as climatic differences between the Chichijima Islands and the Hahajima Islands, the timing of the invasion by invasive rodents in the satellite islands of Hahajima, and geographical factors. Based on a comparative analysis of the Chichijima individual of RrC, we concluded that RrC II (corresponding to Rattus tanezumi) inhabits Katsuodorijima. The previous study reported that RrC II inhabits Hahajima; therefore, we considered that RrC II migrated from Hahajima to Katsuodorijima by swimming because Katsuodorijima is geographically adjacent to Hahajima and can be reached by swimming. In this study, unique haplotypes (CT6, CT8, and TC7) in R. norvegicus at Meijima and Mukohjima, based on the D‐loop analysis, were observed. To the best of our knowledge, these unique haplotypes have not been reported in previous studies; therefore, we considered that these haplotypes originated on Mukohjima and Meijima. Based on this result, although the use of mtDNA data to demonstrate whether migration occurred would be difficult, we suggested that R. norvegicus likely did not migrate from Meijima or Mukohjima to other islands. Invasive rodents severely affect the ecosystems of the Ogasawara Islands, including the Hahajima Islands. Predation of Ogasawara Greenfinch (Chloris kittlitzi) nests is a representative problem. This study provides helpful information for promoting effective invasive rodent control on the Hahajima Islands.

articles.title: Influence of Foraging Effort and Diet on Maternal Energy Stores and Offspring Weaning Mass in Gray Seals (Halichoerus grypus)
articles.abstract: Understanding how foraging behavior and diet influence individual reproductive success is a key interest in evolutionary ecology. This is particularly true for capital breeding species where the accumulation and storage of energy to support offspring is critical, often following the “bigger‐is‐better” hypothesis. Using data collected from female gray seals (Halichoerus grypus) at Sable Island, Canada, between 1995 and 2018, we tested the hypothesis that differences in foraging effort and diet prior to the breeding season, estimated through satellite telemetry, stable isotope (SI) signatures, and quantitative fatty acid signature analysis (QFASA), respectively, affect reproductive success. There was no relationship between dominant prey type, the energy density of estimated diets, and maternal postpartum mass (MPPM). Females consuming a diet of lower diversity and with more positive δ13C estimates, possibly indicating more benthic foraging, had higher MPPM. MPPM was the best predictor of offspring mass at weaning. However, metrics of maternal foraging effort and diet alone did not influence pup weaning mass when MPPM was included in the model. These results suggest that different foraging strategies and diets can lead to sufficient body energy storage that enables reproductive success in a capital breeder. Considering this colony was increasing rapidly during the study period, the influence of foraging effort and diet might differ in a stable or declining population where intraspecific competition may be more evident.

articles.title: Interspecific Cohabitation and Associated Zoonotic Risk in the Burrows of Niokolo‐Koba National Park, Senegal
articles.abstract: In arid and semi‐arid ecosystems, burrows serve as vital sanctuaries providing wildlife shelter, nourishment, and thermal buffering. These benefits attract multiple species into confined spaces, potentially facilitating interspecific pathogen transmission. This study provides a comprehensive assessment of burrow use in Senegal's Niokolo‐Koba National Park, quantifying interspecific cohabitation, identifying influential characteristics, and documenting the potential for zoonotic pathogen transmission. Data were collected during two dry‐season campaigns, which included semi‐opportunistic searches of burrows for camera‐trap monitoring and collection of fecal and tick samples. Cameras detected entering species while samples targeted bacteria with zoonotic potential. Across 1519 camera‐trap days, 32 species were detected using burrows, generating 172 interspecific cohabitations. Each cohabitation represented a species pair entering at least one common entrance during monitoring. An average of 6 different cohabitations per entrance over 20 days was recorded, with a maximum of 5 species visiting the same entrance within 24 h. Occupation occurred in rapid succession rather than simultaneously. Twenty significant preferential cohabitations were identified, ranging from ecological partnerships to predator–prey co‐occurrences. Based on the characteristics recorded for 105 monitored entrances, larger entrance diameter, higher woody cover, and location in valleys were associated with higher cohabitation rates. Pathogen screening detected potential zoonotic bacteria, including Treponema. Ticks were found in half of sampled burrows, with Francisella consistently detected. Results underline the dual ecological and epidemiological roles of burrows, emphasizing the need to integrate One Health considerations into burrow conservation.

articles.title: Lights Out in the Canopy: Arboreal Camera Traps Offer New Insights Into Sleeping‐Site Partitioning and Sleep Ecology in Primate Communities
articles.abstract: Sleep is an essential yet costly biological process, leaving animals vulnerable to predation and constraining their use of space and time. Optimal sleeping sites therefore represent valuable, potentially contested resources, yet they remain largely overlooked in primate community ecology. Understanding how syntopic species compete for and partition sleeping sites can reveal mechanisms of coexistence, but community‐level studies remain limited because multiple arboreal species are difficult to monitor simultaneously. Here, we used arboreal camera traps to investigate sleeping‐site use and spatiotemporal partitioning within a Brazilian Atlantic Forest primate community. Over 7 months (2024–2025), we monitored ten Copaifera trapezifolia trees used as preferred sleeping sites by southern muriquis (Brachyteles arachnoides), brown howler monkeys (Alouatta guariba) and black‐tufted capuchins (Sapajus nigritus cucullatus), recording 4195 videos documenting 1253 visits and 158 sleeping nights. C. trapezifolia trees constituted a shared but limited resource, and access reflected predicted interspecific differences in resource holding potential (RHP), the relative ability of a species to prevail in direct contests over a shared resource. Muriquis and capuchins, the higher‐RHP species with larger home ranges, showed high temporal overlap in copaíba use—preferentially sleeping there on warmer nights and under lower lunar illumination, suggesting roles for thermoregulation and perceived predation risk—offset by reduced spatial overlap, consistent with greater ranging flexibility enabling spatial avoidance. Howlers, constrained by more restricted ranging and repeatedly displaced in direct encounters with the other species, instead relied on temporal segregation to access the same preferred trees. Nocturnal videos further revealed activity beyond residual wakefulness at the edges of the night, offering rare direct evidence of nocturnal behaviour and fragmented sleep in wild arboreal primates. These findings indicate that sleeping sites can function as contested, high‐value resources structuring primate community dynamics through asymmetric contest competition, and highlight arboreal camera trapping as a powerful tool for studying primate sleep ecology.

articles.title: Molecular Adaptations and Sex‐Biased Regulatory Pathways in Multi‐Year Diapause of the Cabbage Beetle Colaphellus bowringi: A Duration‐Resolved Transcriptomic Analysis
articles.abstract: The cabbage beetle Colaphellus bowringi, a key pest of cruciferous crops, exhibits a multiyear dormancy strategy characterized by pronounced interindividual variation in diapause duration: individuals entering summer or winter diapause—though initiated synchronously within each seasonal cohort—may remain in diapause for periods ranging from several months to as long as 5 years. To elucidate the molecular underpinnings of this extended dormancy and its sex‐specific regulatory patterns, we performed a duration‐resolved, sex‐stratified transcriptomic analysis. Adult males and females were sampled after 0.5, 1, and 2 years of diapause durations and subjected to high‐throughput RNA sequencing. De novo assembly yielded 66,379 unigenes, of which 16,132 (24.3%) were removed as non‐arthropod contamination, leaving 50,247 unigenes that were used for all downstream annotation and expression analyses. Comparative transcriptomic profiling revealed a conserved adaptive strategy during prolonged diapause: patterns consistent with coordinated suppression of energy‐intensive metabolic processes coupled with increased transcript abundance of genes in cellular protection pathways—including antioxidant defense, xenobiotic detoxification, and protein homeostasis mechanisms. Sex‐biased transcriptional responses were observed: females showed comparable or higher numbers of differentially expressed genes in matched duration comparisons, with sustained transcript abundance of genes associated with reproductive processes and somatic maintenance, whereas males displayed greater duration‐dependent transcriptional remodeling, particularly in signaling cascades and physiological homeostasis networks. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis identified sustained activation of glutathione metabolism, autophagy, and lysosomal degradation pathways throughout diapause; notably, extended diapause (2 years) was specifically associated with significant enrichment of immune response and lipid metabolism pathways. Duration‐dependent dynamics in gene expression underscore that diapause is not a static quiescent state but a highly regulated, multi‐stage process involving duration‐specific transcriptional reconfiguration. This study establishes the first duration‐resolved, sex‐resolved transcriptomic resource for C. bowringi and advances mechanistic understanding of long‐term insect diapause—thereby informing the development of targeted, environmentally sustainable pest management strategies.

articles.title: Nanoplastic Exposure Impairs Host Fitness and Parasite Transmission With Transgenerational Maternal Reproductive Costs in the Daphnia‐Fungal Parasite System
articles.abstract: Nanoplastics are emerging contaminants in aquatic ecosystems, but their direct and maternally transmitted effects on host–parasite interactions remain poorly understood. We investigated the effects of polystyrene nanoplastic exposure (50 nm, 5 mg L−1) on Daphnia magna infected with the fungal parasite Australozyma monospora across two host generations. Direct nanoplastic exposure occurred in the parental generation (F0), whereas F1 offspring were raised in nanoplastic‐free medium to isolate maternal nanoplastic effects. Direct nanoplastic exposure severely impaired F0 host fitness, reduced reproductive probability and total offspring production, while halving median survival time relative to controls. Nanoplastic exposure also impaired parasite maturation likelihood by decreasing host survival prior to transmission. Infection prevalence and spore production did not differ between nanoplastic‐exposed and control hosts among individuals that survived to the transmission stage, suggesting that nanoplastic exposure compromises parasite fitness primarily through accelerated host mortality rather than through within‐host suppression. In the F1 generation, offspring of nanoplastic‐exposed mothers had lower reproductive probability and delayed age at first clutch, despite experiencing no direct nanoplastic exposure. Host survival and parasite fitness outcomes were not altered in F1. Together, these results demonstrate that nanoplastic pollution disrupts host–parasite dynamics both directly and across generations, imposing reproductive costs that persist in unexposed offspring through maternal effects. Such transgenerational effects compromise host population recovery and amplify parasite transmission in nanoplastic‐contaminated freshwater environments.

articles.title: Preliminary Evidence Suggests the Transcriptomic Response of Tricolored Bats to White‐Nose Syndrome Is Similar but Not Identical to That of Little Brown Bats
articles.abstract: Understanding the pathophysiology of emerging wildlife diseases can inform treatment, improve the projections of long‐term population trajectories, and reveal variation in population‐level impacts among species. Research on white‐nose syndrome (WNS) in hibernating North American bats has largely focused on a single highly susceptible species, the little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus). Another susceptible species, the tricolored bat (Perimyotis subflavus), has experienced population declines comparable to or greater than those of little brown bats but remains understudied. In particular, the immune response of tricolored bats to WNS has not previously been evaluated. Here, we conduct a preliminary analysis comparing part of the transcriptomic response of tricolored bats to WNS with the little brown bat response. We analyzed 14 tricolored and 13 little brown bat samples collected from Colossal Cave, Kentucky, USA in 2017, where WNS has been present since 2013. We also included 26 little brown bat samples collected from a nearby hibernation site in 1999, prior to WNS emergence. Lacking a proper pre‐WNS control for tricolored bats, we conducted pairwise differential expression analyses between the three sample groups and evaluated the overlap between results to infer part of the tricolored bat response to WNS. These initial results suggested that tricolored bats exhibited differential expression patterns characteristic of susceptible species, including large changes in gene expression still apparent at the end of the hibernation season. Differentially expressed genes were associated with immune, metabolic, and circadian functions, broadly resembling the response observed in little brown bats. However, there was variation in the specific genes involved between the two species. Overall, tricolored bats appear to mount a pronounced immune response to WNS that is similar, but not identical, to that of little brown bats.

articles.title: Roe Deer Capreolus capreolus Home Range Size and Daily Distance in the Agricultural Landscape of East‐Central Poland in Relation to Natural and Anthropogenic Factors
articles.abstract: The home ranges, core areas, and daily distances traveled of 10 collared roe deer in the agricultural landscape of east‐central Poland were analyzed. We demonstrated the dependence of the home range size and daily distance on natural and anthropogenic factors. We first demonstrated a relationship between home range size and the wind farm impacts on roe deer.ABSTRACTHome range and daily distance traveled are the basic parameters of animal habitat utilization and emerge from complex interactions between animals and their environment. In this study, the home ranges, core areas, and daily distances traveled of 10 collared roe deer in east‐central Poland were analyzed. The mean home range size for all animals was 136.1 ha (minimum convex polygon of 95% of points), and 69 ha (95% kernel density estimation); the mean core area was 10.9 ha (50% kernel density estimation). Core areas were larger in males than in females and larger in the winter period than in the growing period. Home range size decreased with increasing forest cover and increased with the number of wind turbines. Core area size was influenced only by the sex of the animal and forest cover. Neither the size of the home range nor the size of the core area depended on road density or settlement cover. The relationship between home range size and sex, natural factors, including forest cover, and season, is consistent with previous studies. Mean daily distance traveled for all animals was 3.14 km, and was lower in the growing period than in winter, and in females than in males. The daily distance traveled also decreased with increasing forest cover. Our study indicated a new anthropogenic factor shaping roe deer's spatial behavior in agricultural landscapes (wind farms). We concluded that roe deer have probably adapted behaviorally to wind farms as a new landscape feature. They probably treat wind farms like human settlements, generally avoid them, and use habitats at an appropriate distance from the turbines. We cannot, however, exclude the occasional fleeing behavior of roe deer near turbines. Further research should include a more detailed assessment of the behavior of roe deer and other terrestrial mammal species under the influence of wind farms.

articles.title: The Impact of Ants and Vertebrate Predators on Arthropods and Plants: A Meta‐Analysis
articles.abstract: The trophic interactions between plants, insect herbivores and their predators are complex and prone to trophic cascades. Theory predicts that predators increase plant biomass by feeding on herbivores. However, it remains unclear whether different types of predators regulate herbivores to the same degree, and how intraguild predation impacts these trophic interactions. Specifically, we lack a more comprehensive view of the effects of various groups of predators on a global scale. Here we report a meta‐analysis of 486 experiments gathered from 157 publications reporting the effect of insectivorous vertebrates (birds and bats) and ants on richness and abundances of all arthropods; predatory (spiders, ants, others) and herbivorous (chewers and others) arthropods; and on plant damage. Generally, the absence of vertebrate predators led to the increase of predatory arthropods by 18%, herbivorous arthropods by 75%, and plant damage by 47%. In contrast, after the removal of ants, the increase in the abundances of other predatory arthropods did not compensate for the missing ants, herbivore arthropods increased their abundances by 53%, and plant damage increased by 146%. Ant exclosure effects were more pronounced at lower elevations and latitudes, whereas vertebrate exclosure did not show any clear geographical patterns. Furthermore, exclusion effects remained robust across various plant growth forms and habitat types, with neither precipitation nor NDVI significantly influencing most observed outcomes. We found vertebrate insectivores to be the more dominant predators of arthropods, but we detected that the strength of their trophic cascades was weakened by intraguild predation. On the other hand, we found that although ants were relatively less dominant as predators, and their influence was detectable only in the most productive sites, the effect of the trophic cascades they caused on plants was stronger than that of vertebrate insectivores.

articles.title: The Role of Chromosomal Fusions in Genetic Divergence of a Keystone Arctic Species (Boreogadus saida)
articles.abstract: Local adaptation in species with high gene flow can be facilitated through different genomic mechanisms. For example, multiple studies have demonstrated that chromosomal inversions (CIs) are important for adaptive divergence in systems with high gene flow because they help protect locally adaptive alleles from recombination. Although much focus has been given to the importance of CIs in harboring adaptive alleles, there are other mechanisms that can facilitate genetic divergence. Chromosomal fusions can also promote local adaptation in the face of high gene flow by bringing together previously unlinked loci. Herein, we utilized a newly available reference genome for Arctic cod (Boreogadus saida), together with whole‐genome sequence data from locations spanning a large portion of the Canadian Arctic, to describe the genomic architecture in this circumpolar fish. The Arctic cod genome contains many CIs and five chromosomes that appear to have undergone lineage‐specific chromosomal fusions. Consistent with previous studies, we documented both high gene flow and signals of non‐neutral divergence at a relatively small subset of loci that are driving local population structure. However, our analyses illustrate that most non‐neutral loci are found on fused chromosomes, suggesting chromosomal fusions might be important for local adaptation in this species. This result is especially notable given the localization of divergence in the fused chromosomes when the Arctic cod genome has numerous CIs that are infrequently utilized for divergence across the locations sampled in this study. Our study strongly suggests that non‐neutral loci are concentrated on chromosomal fusions, which may facilitate localized adaptation despite high levels of gene flow in a non‐model species.

articles.title: The Spring Phenology of Arboreal Beetles and Spiders and Their Potential as Alternative Prey for Birds Mistimed With Peak Caterpillar Abundance
articles.abstract: The match/mismatch hypothesis (MMH) predicts that consumers that are asynchronous with a key ephemeral resource will have reduced fitness. However, by diet‐switching to an alternative resource with which it is synchronous, a consumer may be able to buffer the negative fitness consequences of asynchrony. The trophic interaction between spring arboreal caterpillars and insectivorous passerine consumers is a well‐established MMH study‐system, though caterpillars are not the only prey guild used. Here, we examine the phenological distribution of beetle and spider abundance, two alternative prey guilds utilised by many breeding passerines. Using data collected across a 220 km transect of Scotland, encompassing 44 mixed deciduous woodland sites, we address four questions: (i) Do beetle and spider abundance show a peaked phenological distribution during spring? (ii) Do the phenological distributions of different taxa vary among years and tree taxa? (iii) Does the overall abundance of either taxon vary among tree taxa or (iv) with temperature? We also compare the average phenological distribution of beetles and spiders to the caterpillar peak, considering whether there is potential for diet‐switching for birds mistimed with the peak in caterpillars. We found beetle abundance consistently peaked in early June, while spider abundance decreased linearly throughout spring. Overall, our results demonstrate both tree taxon‐specific and annual variation in the abundance and phenological distributions of both alternative prey guilds, with spider abundance also increasing with spring temperature. Our results demonstrate the potential for diet‐switching for mistimed birds, as the abundance of beetles was consistently higher than caterpillars throughout spring and spider abundance was higher earlier in the season, prior to the peak in caterpillars.
